newsitem.title: FRANCE: French prosecutor wants Scientologists fined.
newsitem.headline: French prosecutor wants Scientologists fined.

text.p: The prosecution asked a court on Monday to sentence 21 members of the French Church of Scientology to suspended jail terms and fines of up to 500,000 francs ($100,000) on charges ranging from fraud to manslaughter.

The prosecution told the court in the central city of Lyon it wanted a three-year suspended sentence to be passed on Jean-Jacques Mazier, former head of the church in France, for manslaughter and fraud in the 1988 suicide of church follower Patrice Vic.
Vic, a 30-year-old industrial designer, plunged to his death from his apartment after being unable to raise the money he needed for a costly church course.

The week-old trial was prompted when Vic's widow Nelly accused the church of driving him into debt and despair. It was brought to trial after the French government announced it was cracking down on cults.
In all, 23 Scientologists were in the dock, variously accused of manslaughter, embezzlement, fraud and complicity.
In addition to Mazier, the prosecution asked for terms of between six months and two years suspended against 20 of the accused and asked that the court show leniency towards two others.
Nelly Vic's lawyer asked the court to grant her and her son 100,000 francs ($20,000) each in damages.
A lawyer for other plaintiffs said the church had infiltrated political, economic and sociological circles to set up a swindle and mafia-type extortion system which he called "a money pump".
During the trial, prosecutors and former members accused the church of exploiting the gullibility of members for commercial profit, through pseudo-scientific and paramedical means.
Debates focused on whether the Church of Scientology, founded in 1954 by the late American science-fiction novelist L. Ron Hubbard, was a sect or a religion.

By winning recognition as a religion, the church could defuse some of the charges because it would have a legal right to appeal to its members for funds. It claims more than eight million adherents worldwide, including 4,000 in France.

One of scientology's teachings is that the problems of the human race are linked to disembodied souls brought to the planet millions of years ago. Church members submit to personality tests and then undergo expensive courses to evict evil spirits.
Members include Hollywood film stars Tom Cruise, Nicole Kidman, John Travolta, Kirstie Alley and Lisa Marie Presley.
Followers are mainly recruited through personality tests and then offered costly books and courses to solve their problems.
The trial was expected to end with defence pleas on Tuesday.
